notes: Compact, deep violet; the classic low hedge. Trim after flowering, never into old wood.
Early, compact, lavender-blue; good for edging. Shear by a third after flowering.
Early blue-violet flowers on a compact bush; trim after flowering to keep it dense.
Pale pink lavender for soft-coloured edging; clip after flowering, never into bare wood.
The Provence field lavandin: long, intensely scented spikes; the best for oil and drying.
Pale lavender, long-stemmed and very fragrant; a lavandin for drying and sachets.
Vigorous, uniform lavandin selected for cold winters and humid summers; silvery all year.
Showy purple 'rabbit-ear' bracts; deadhead for repeat flowering. Dislikes winter wet.
Toothed grey leaves; flowers most of the year in mild climates. Overwinter frost-free elsewhere.
Broad grey leaves and branched, camphor-scented spikes in late summer. Lean, limy soil.
Papery magenta flowers with a dark blotch, each lasting a day. Trim lightly after flowering only.
White-felted leaves and soft lilac-pink flowers; loves lime and heat, resents hard pruning.
Low and spreading, one of the hardiest cistus; white flowers with a yellow eye. Good on banks.
Sticky, aromatic leaves; huge white flowers with maroon blotches. Short-lived, needs drainage.
Low grey-green mound with vivid cerise flowers for weeks; great on sunny banks and walls.
Hardiest common cistus: white flowers from crimson buds, leaves bronze in winter. Syn. C. × corbariensis.
Grey downy leaves and yellow saucers with maroon spots in late spring; needs lean, sharp soil.
Clip in spring for a tight silver edging; shear off the flowers if grown for foliage.
Bright green thread-like leaves and lemon buttons; clip as a low hedge in spring.
Whorls of hooded yellow flowers over woolly grey leaves; prune lightly after flowering.
Stacked whorls of butter-yellow hoods; seedheads stand all winter. Weed-smothering leaves.
Cut flowered stems to the base after flowering. Milky sap irritates skin and eyes.
Trailing blue-grey stems for walls and gravel; self-seeds. Sap irritant – wear gloves.
Stiff blue-grey stems topped with bright yellow in early spring; leaves blush red in heat.
Silver needles smelling of curry; mustard buttons in summer. Trim in spring, not into old wood.
Fast silver-white hedge with pale blue flowers through summer; clip after flowering.
Glossy evergreen edging for knots and gravel; pink flowers loved by bees. Clip in spring.
Aromatic leaves, fluffy white flowers, blue-black berries. Clips well; a tub plant where cold.
Compact, small-leaved myrtle for low hedges and topiary balls; white flowers in late summer.
All parts highly toxic. Where winters are cold, grow in tubs and overwinter bright at 5–10 °C.
Orange-blossom-scented flowers in late spring; superb salt-tolerant hedge or screen.
Dense evergreen dome that needs almost no clipping; good filler for pots and seaside beds.
Rosemary look-alike, unscented; shrugs off salt wind. Clips into neat hedges and balls.
Scented yellow pea flowers from late winter; best against a warm wall in colder areas.
Rush-like green stems with honey-scented yellow flowers all summer; may self-seed. Toxic.
Spiny cushion smothered in yellow in late spring; lean soil, resents transplanting.
Woolly white-felted stems grown for foliage; cut back in spring. Hates winter wet.
Tough blue-green evergreen with yellow-green umbels in late summer; takes salt wind and chalk.
Silver, salt-proof hedge for seaside gardens; clip in spring. Flowers insignificant.
Feathery silver foliage; cut back to new shoots in spring. Rarely flowers; hates winter wet.
Aromatic silver farm-garden herb; cut back in spring. Bitter and toxic in quantity.
Hazy blue spires over white stems; cut back to 30 cm in spring. Syn. Perovskia 'Blue Spire'.
Flowers June to frost; shorten by a third in spring. Needs sharp drainage to survive winter.
Bushy, with crimson flowers June to frost; leaves smell of blackcurrant. Prune in spring.
Deep purple flowers in near-black calyces until frost; mulch the crown or take cuttings.
Biennial: leaf rosette in year one, then lilac-pink bracts; self-seeds. Pungent scent.
Silky silver leaves and white funnels from pink buds; needs sharp drainage and shelter.
Trailing lavender-blue funnels all summer for walls and pots; tender in wet winters.
Container plant: overwinter frost-free and bright. Berries toxic; invasive in the tropics.
Sky-blue flowers all summer on a scrambling shrub; tie in. Overwinter frost-free in tubs.
Crimson bottlebrushes in early summer, lemon-scented leaves. Tub plant in cold areas.
Glossy, salt- and drought-proof evergreen screen; berries for birds. Clips well.
Resinous evergreen of the maquis; dense hedge for hot, salty sites. Red then black berries.
Pink spikes fading to white all summer; good by the sea. Trim lightly after flowering.
Grey-green leaves edged red, redder in winter; lilac flowers. Neat, hardy, salt-tolerant.
Evergreen; flowers best when pot-bound. Where frosty, overwinter frost-free and fairly dry.
Hardier deciduous strain; mulch crowns in winter. Plant slightly crowded in full sun.
Airy white flowers June to frost; short-lived, needs drainage. Syn. Gaura lindheimeri.
Daisy froth for steps and wall cracks, May to frost; self-seeds freely. Shear in spring.
Thrives in walls and poor chalky soil; cut back after the first flush for more. Self-seeds.
Sulphur-yellow plates over silver ferny leaves; dries well. Divide every 3 years.
Felted silver carpet; cut off the flower spikes for a tidier mat. Rots in heavy wet soil.
Silver-veined leaves and steel-blue thistle heads; deep taproot, don't move. Dries well.
Biennial: silver bracts in its second summer, then dies; scatter seed where you want it.
See-through purple heads on wiry stems, fine at the front of beds. Self-seeds where happy.
Silver felt rosettes, vivid magenta flowers; short-lived but self-seeds. Syn. Lychnis coronaria.
Blue-grey rosettes and yellow poppies on shingle; short-lived, self-seeds. Toxic.
Scarlet tubes from late summer into autumn; needs a hot, dry spot. Syn. Zauschneria.
Butterfly magnet; purple-flushed leaves in cool weather. Leave seedheads, cut back in spring.
Cut back after the first flush in July for a second show. Not low despite the name.
Blue-grey grassy tufts and dense yellow spikes; ornamental seed pods. Lean, dry soil.
Spikes of brown-veined white stars over grassy leaves; summer-dormant in hot, dry places.
Bold glossy leaves of classical capitals; deep roots make it hard to remove once planted.
Clouds of tiny lavender flowers that dry for bouquets. Deep taproot – don't move. Syn. L. latifolium.
Dense cushions with pink drumsticks; tolerates salt spray. Deadhead to prolong flowering.
Golden spring cushions for walls and rockeries; trim after flowering to keep compact.
Silver mat with white stars in late spring; vigorous, can swamp small neighbours.
Evergreen dark cushions covered in white in April; shear lightly after flowering.
Mats of mauve-pink daisies that open in sun; one of the hardier osteospermums.
Flowers open only in sun. Perennial in frost-free coastal gardens, summer bedding elsewhere.
Succulent mat with shimmering magenta daisies all summer; sharp drainage, no winter wet.
Glossy near-black rosettes; container plant, overwinter bright above 5 °C. Water sparingly.
Huge blue rosettes with vicious spines – keep away from paths. Dies after flowering.
Hardy evergreen rosettes; ivory bells on 1.5 m spikes in July. Remove spent rosettes.
Stiff, sharp-tipped leaves on a short trunk; ivory spikes in late summer. Takes salt wind.
Iconic Mediterranean cactus with edible fruit; fine glochids irritate skin. Needs heat.
Winter-hardy cactus: pads shrivel in frost, then plump up. Needs gravel and no winter wet.
Tiny succulent carpet for roofs, walls and paving; reddens in drought. White stars in June.
Rosettes multiply into mats; flowering rosettes die. Traditional on roofs and walls.
Glaucous cabbage-like leaves, honey-scented white clouds; blanched spring shoots are edible.
Long-flowering bee magnet with anise-scented leaves; leave stems over winter, cut in spring.
Silky blond tufts that sway in the breeze; comb out in spring. Self-seeds. Syn. Stipa tenuissima.
Golden oat-like panicles to 2 m, yet see-through; comb out dead leaves in spring.
Steel-blue evergreen fountain; comb out dead leaves in spring rather than cutting back.
Fluffy creamy plumes July to frost; often grown as an annual. Syn. Cenchrus longisetus.
Hardy annual: sow in spring or autumn where it is to flower. Fluffy heads dry well.
Huge evergreen tussock with arching one-sided plumes; leaf edges cut skin – wear gloves.
Annual with dangling lockets that tremble in the wind; sow where it is to grow. Dries well.
Egg-shaped maroon drumsticks in July; plant in drifts through grasses. Cheap and reliable.
Metallic lilac globes 20 cm across; seedheads last for months. Leaves fade at flowering.
Nodding cream-and-plum bells, then upright seedheads; self-seeds. Syn. Nectaroscordum siculum.
Tiny violet irises in February; plant 8 cm deep in sharp drainage. Often fades after year two.
Hardy magenta gladiolus that naturalises in sunny borders; plant corms 10 cm deep in autumn.

origin: S Europe, N Africa, W Asia
notes: Scented, nodding yellow tulip of old vineyards; spreads by stolons in sunny grass.
Slender white tulip striped red outside; perennialises in hot, sharply drained spots.
Pick the three red stigmas in October for saffron; plant corms 10 cm deep in August.
Clusters of very fragrant white-and-gold flowers; needs a hot, dry summer rest to reflower.
Crocus-like golden goblets in autumn; plant shallow in a hot, dry spot and leave alone.
Soak corms before planting; mulch in winter, or plant in spring where winters are cold.
Pink flowers in late summer, then marbled leaves all winter. Thrives in dry shade under trees.
